In the mid/upper-levels, split-flow persists across the Lower 48, 
with a pair of shortwave troughs ejecting over the northern Great 
Plains and the ARK-LA-TEX region. The leading edge of an enormous 
baroclinic leaf continues to advect poleward over the Eastern 
Seaboard, as the southern-stream, shortwave trough ejecting over the 
ARK-LA-TEX region has induced concavity to the exit-region of the 
subtropical jet stream stretched across Mexico and into the northern 
Gulf Coast. A low-amplitude, shortwave ridge was sandwiched between 
these aforementioned features, and will continue to shift quickly 
eastward over the CWA today as the upstream troughs begin to phase 
into a highly-amplified and closed, negatively-tilted trough over 
the Thanksgiving holiday. The sky was clear across the CWA this 
morning as a result of the shortwave ridge, with the mid-level core 
of a polar anticyclone rotating into southern New England. Easterly 
winds on the southern periphery of this anticyclone has kept the 
airmass from decoupling over the higher terrain, keeping winds 
elevated across those locales where gusts to 20 mph will be common 
throughout the remainder of the morning. The northern edge of a 
lower-level cloud deck advecting poleward towards the Ohio River 
Valley, and will arrive this evening. River valley fog is not 
expected this morning due to the dry state of the airmass.

At the surface, a polar anticyclone, analyzed at 1040 mb, was 
rotating eastward into New England. An inverted surface trough 
extends from the centroid of the polar high southeastward into 
the northern Gulf Basin where it connects to a surface low, the 
latter of which will phase with another cyclone rotating off of 
the GA/SC coastline. Cold temperatures were present across the 
region, with much warmer temperatures in store this afternoon
due to the effects of compressional warming from the downsloping 
winds off of the mountains. Clouds will advect poleward later this 
morning and into the afternoon, with ceilings lowering this evening 
as vigorous and moist, isentropic ascent overspreads the entire 
region heading into tonight. Rapid deepening of the surface low is 
expected to occur as it moves inland from the Atlantic Ocean due to 
steep, geopotential height falls on the order of 120 m/12 hr as the 
shortwave troughs begin to phase over the Mid-Atlantic region. The 
25/00Z RAOBs over the southern Great Plains observed geopotential 
height falls of 40-70 m compared to 12 hours prior, signifying that 
the intensity of the geopotential height falls are a certainty at 
this point in the forecast. This will generate a strong, isallobaric 
response as the attendant surface low deepens and rotates poleward 
along the Appalachian Mountains while becoming vertically-stacked 
after the phasing of the troughs is completed. 

A High Wind Warning is now in effect for the ridges across the 
northeastern mountains of WV, with a Wind Advisory adjacent to the 
zones within the High Wind Warning, both of which are in effect from 
26/06Z-27/00Z, or 1 AM EST Thursday through 7 PM EST Thursday. There 
is high confidence in the potential for a prolonged period of wind 
gusts up to 50-55 mph and 60 mph across the advisory and warning
areas, respectively; and it is possible that localized wind gusts 
may reach 65 mph for locales within the High Wind Warning. Wind 
gusts were nudged slightly upward from the NBM using a blend of the 
NBM 90th percentile; however, wind gusts were capped at 53 kt, which 
is in the middle of the upper echelon gusts initialized by the NBM 
90th percentile. Additional upward adjustments to the wind gust 
factor may be necessary in forthcoming shifts. Winds are forecast to 
peak in intensity during the morning hours on Thanksgiving, with 
winds gradually subsiding thereafter as the core of the aligning 
vortex rotates over the region. Elsewhere, blustery, northeasterly 
winds are expected for Thanksgiving. 

Widespread rainfall will last for all of Thanksgiving Day and into 
the night, with a changeover to a wintry mix in the mountains and 
possibly portions of the lowlands by Friday morning. Accumulations 
of snow are not expected in the lower elevations should a rain-snow 
mix occur. As the transition from rain to mixed-phased precipitation 
evolves in the higher terrain, there exists the possibility for 
freezing rain, which may result in a glaze of ice on elevated 
surfaces due to temperatures Friday morning being slightly colder 
than the prior forecasts. However, ice accretion will be limited due 
to the locally heavier precipitation rates within the evolving 
upslope flow regime, in addition the latent heat release from the 
supercooled droplets resulting in marginally-freezing temperatures 
rising back to near 32 degrees before a complete transition to snow 
develops by late Friday morning. The core of the negatively-tilted 
trough and vertically-stacked cyclone will quickly progress to the
